main_changes.before: To identify the optimal descriptor for downstream expert-guided learning, we benchmarked four molecular representations under a unified 5-fold stratified cross-validation protocol: transformer-based embeddings (MolFormer, 768-dimensional; ChemBERTa) and classical fingerprints (Morgan, MACCS). MolFormer embeddings consistently outperformed all alternatives, achieving the highest mean F1-score of 0.655 (MLP with StandardScaler) and accuracy of 0.856, whereas Morgan, MACCS, and ChemBERTa exhibited near-random F1 scores (≤0.50) despite moderate accuracy (Figure SI 1-2). This accuracy–F1 divergence indicates that classical fingerprints and the smaller chemical language model capture majority-class bias rather than biocide-specific structural motifs, whereas MolFormer’s pre-trained chemical vocabulary already encodes the subtle physicochemical nuances relevant to membrane-targeting cationics. Detailed per-representation and per-scaler comparisons are provided in the Supporting Information.
main_changes.after: To identify the optimal descriptor for downstream expert-guided learning, we benchmarked four molecular representations under a unified 5-fold stratified cross-validation protocol: transformer-based embeddings (MolFormer, 768-dimensional; ChemBERTa) and classical fingerprints (Morgan, MACCS). MolFormer embeddings consistently outperformed all alternatives, achieving the highest mean F1-score of 0.655 (MLP with StandardScaler) and accuracy of 0.856, whereas Morgan, MACCS, and ChemBERTa exhibited near-random F1 scores (≤0.50) despite moderate accuracy (Figures S1–S2). This accuracy–F1 divergence indicates that classical fingerprints and the smaller chemical language model capture majority-class bias rather than biocide-specific structural motifs, whereas MolFormer’s pre-trained chemical vocabulary already encodes the subtle physicochemical nuances relevant to membrane-targeting cationics. Detailed per-representation and per-scaler comparisons are provided in the Supporting Information.

main_changes.before: Having obtained the embeddings, we next evaluated them on the MIC and MBC regression tasks for the 105 quaternary ammonium compounds introduced in our previous work. Each molecule is represented together with the bacterial species and activity type, allowing a shared CatBoost model to predict four quantitative endpoints. Expert Good/Bad labels train the representation; measured MIC/MBC values still train the downstream quantitative decoder. Complete reference results are provided in Tables S45–S46.

main_changes.before: The original reference comparison shows the value of this task-aware formulation. With human-guided molecular features and text-encoded task descriptions, the recovered endpoint R² values are 0.75, 0.68, 0.59 and 0.77 for S. aureus MIC, S. aureus MBC, E. coli MIC and E. coli MBC, respectively. One-hot and categorical task coding provide simpler alternatives. Text descriptions are encoded with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, giving one fixed 1,536-dimensional vector for each of the four species–endpoint combinations; exact inputs and cache provenance are provided in SI Section S34. The original comparison also reports close point estimates for the expert-guided and full-corpus quantitative encoders (Table S46), suggesting that coarse expert supervision can produce useful molecular features. Similar scores do not by themselves establish equivalence of the two sources or demonstrate a unique semantic benefit of text task descriptions.

main_changes.before: To assess variability separately from these historical holdout results, we reconstructed five-fold row-wise cross-validation using the saved human-guided features and recovered decoder budget. Cation and scaffold holdouts address the different question of prediction for new molecular groups.

main_changes.before: The violins in Figure 5 show the observed endpoint-error distributions on the same 105 salts. Median absolute errors are 1.18, 1.08, 1.14 and 1.18 log₂ units for human, quantitative, shuffled-human and raw MolFormer features under cation holdout, and 1.42, 1.36, 1.30 and 1.38 under scaffold holdout. Human and quantitative guidance give similar pooled errors, with their ordering depending on the holdout scheme. Shuffled-human guidance remains competitive in this compact-encoder experiment, limiting claims that human-label meaning uniquely explains the result. Detailed seed statistics and controls are in Table S41. These comparisons assess representation-learning procedures; an expert label is not assumed to be informationally equivalent to an individual concentration measurement.

main_changes.before: Modern molecular and tabular models provide additional checks on the choice of decoder. Chemprop, TabPFN, TabFM and AutoGluon were evaluated on the same target registers. TabFM improves the separate-endpoint raw CatBoost pipeline in the grouped point comparisons, illustrating that the best procedure depends on both representation and decoder. Different PCA treatments and optimisation budgets make these practical pipeline comparisons. Full endpoint results and fold variability are provided in Tables S38 and S42.

main_changes.before: On Q-HERO, human guidance also exceeds shuffled-human guidance (AUROC 0.567 ± 0.070). The paired difference is +0.108, with conditional 95% bootstrap interval [0.031, 0.237] over source/decoder seeds and scaffold clusters. The human−RF contrast is positive under scaffold evaluation (+0.110 [0.026, 0.201]), while its random-test interval includes zero [−0.066, 0.297]. This supports a contribution from label assignment in the stated procedure, without establishing a biological mechanism or superiority over quantitative guidance. The ± values denote sample SD of five complete runs. Since 360 of 405 molecules are active, precision–recall results are interpreted against the high positive-class prevalence. Full metrics, controls and provenance are in Tables S47–S48. The matched RF comparison concerns our cleaned cohort and scaffold protocol, rather than the authors’ original 421-row random test.

main_changes.before: However, despite the well-known nature of the method, we encountered several unexpected difficulties during the implementation of the process requiring optimization of the MCR synthesis conditions. First, the desired THP was produced in mixture with 4H-pyran as a result of a competitive process of intramolecular cyclization via the attack of carbonyl on the nitrile group after Michael addition (Scheme S1). The MCR conditions for a 3-pyridinecarboxaldehyde, malononitrile, methyl acetoacetate and ammonium acetate were optimized by varying the solvent, temperature, and the equivalents of ammonium acetate (Table S1). 4H-Pyran was the primary product during the reaction at room temperature, while at 64 ℃ and increased solvent load the quantity of the by-product slightly decreased (Table S1 entry 3). As the amount of NH4OAc increases to 4.0 mol. equiv., the reaction’s sole product is desired THP. Consequently, we attempted to conduct the reaction using ethanol, which is less hazardous to human health and is classified as a green solvent 70. Carrying out a similar reaction in ethanol at 78 ℃ resulted in 62% yield of the desired THP (Table S1 entry 7). Second, the Menshutkin reaction led to the formation of bis-QAC in the form of a pair of diastereoisomers (Scheme S2). In our previous study, we found that 4SR,6RS-THP convert to more stable epimers when heated in DMSO. Thus, we carried out additional epimerization step in order to obtain a more diastereoselectively pure product. The subsequent Menshutkin reaction yielded bis-pyridinium salts in the form of a single diastereomer.
main_changes.after: However, despite the well-known nature of the method, we encountered several unexpected difficulties during the implementation of the process requiring optimization of the MCR synthesis conditions. First, the desired THP was produced in mixture with 4H-pyran as a result of a competitive process of intramolecular cyclization via the attack of carbonyl on the nitrile group after Michael addition (Scheme S1). The MCR conditions for a 3-pyridinecarboxaldehyde, malononitrile, methyl acetoacetate and ammonium acetate were optimized by varying the solvent, temperature, and the equivalents of ammonium acetate (Table S13). 4H-Pyran was the primary product during the reaction at room temperature, while at 64 ℃ and increased solvent load the quantity of the by-product slightly decreased (Table S13 entry 3). As the amount of NH4OAc increases to 4.0 mol. equiv., the reaction’s sole product is desired THP. Consequently, we attempted to conduct the reaction using ethanol, which is less hazardous to human health and is classified as a green solvent 70. Carrying out a similar reaction in ethanol at 78 ℃ resulted in 62% yield of the desired THP (Table S13 entry 7). Second, the Menshutkin reaction led to the formation of bis-QAC in the form of a pair of diastereoisomers (Scheme S2). In our previous study, we found that 4SR,6RS-THP convert to more stable epimers when heated in DMSO. Thus, we carried out additional epimerization step in order to obtain a more diastereoselectively pure product. The subsequent Menshutkin reaction yielded bis-pyridinium salts in the form of a single diastereomer.

main_changes.before: In the archived concatenated-feature CatBoost model, summed mean absolute SHAP values on the 67 exact OOD endpoints are 2.930 for MolFormer features, 0.636 for human features and 0.761 for the task identifier. The human-to-MolFormer block ratio is 0.217. These attributions describe how that fitted model allocates prediction contributions among correlated feature blocks of different dimensions. They are neither fractions of biological variance nor evidence for a separate causal knowledge channel. Detailed archived geometry and attribution results remain in SI, together with the original conceptual diagram in Figure S34.

main_changes.before: Weight interventions provide a complementary check. Restoring source encoder weights in the partial-backbone experiment raises cation-held-out RMSE by +0.109, conditional interval [+0.037, +0.201], while scaffold and four-family OOD intervals include zero. The compact weight-reset experiment does not resolve a corresponding effect and retains BatchNorm state, so it is distinct from an entirely untrained encoder. Figure S35 and Table S50 show the full contrasts for both architectures. Such interventions address dependence of the prediction procedure on learned updates, rather than a causal effect of a molecular fragment on antibacterial activity.
